say.text: A classmate says: 'Every intestinal obstruction gives the same features in the same order, so the level of the block changes nothing.' Many students hold this view.
Do you agree with your classmate?

choices.label: The same features, in the same order, at any level
The order shifts with where the block sits

say.text: Tempting, because the four cardinal features are the same for every block, so one timeline feels natural.
But the timing follows the bowel on each side of the block. Above it the bowel dilates; below it the bowel empties and collapses.
So the level changes the order of the features, not the list. Next you will test this on a case.

sure_note.text: You were sure the level makes no difference. Keep this: the four features stay the same, but their order depends on the level.

say.text: Right. The level sets the order. Above a block the bowel keeps filling; below it the bowel empties first.
A high small bowel block vomits early and distends little (K51, K53).
A low small bowel or large bowel block vomits late and distends markedly, with the vomit turning faeculent later.
Constipation follows the bowel below the block. In a large bowel block absolute constipation comes early, because the distal bowel empties first (K54).
Now test the idea on a case. A large bowel obstruction, early in the course.
Which feature set fits best?

choices.label: Early profuse vomiting, minimal distension, late constipation
Early absolute constipation, marked distension, late vomiting
Early vomiting, marked distension, early constipation
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which part of the bowel is still emptying, and how much of it sits below the block.
That set is the high small bowel pattern. It tempts because vomiting-first is the picture you learn first (K51).
Hint: ask how much bowel lies below this block, and which part empties first.
Distension is tempting here because it is marked in a large block (K53). But the pairing feels right and one feature sits in the wrong place (K51).
Hint: check each feature against the bowel below the block. Which one needs that bowel to empty first?
Same case, second look. Which set fits the large bowel block?

choices.label: Early vomiting, marked distension, early constipation
Early profuse vomiting, minimal distension, late constipation
Early absolute constipation, marked distension, late vomiting

say.text: Tempting: profuse early vomiting with minimal distension is the high small bowel picture, and it may be the set you learnt first.
Here the block sits low, so vomiting comes late and distension is marked (K51, K53).
What is right: early absolute constipation, marked distension, late vomiting. The bowel below the block empties first, so constipation comes early (K54).

sure_note.text: You were sure of the high small bowel set. Keep the rule: the level decides which feature comes first.

say.text: Tempting: marked distension and early constipation both fit a large block, so the mixed set looks plausible.
But vomiting is late in a large bowel block, not early (K51).
What is right: early absolute constipation, marked distension, late vomiting.

sure_note.text: You were sure of the mixed set. Vomiting is the feature that moves late in a low block; that is the detail to fix.

say.text: Right. The distal bowel empties first, so absolute constipation comes early, with marked distension and late vomiting (K54, K53, K51).
A mechanical obstruction is a fixed block, and peristalsis keeps pushing against it (K12).
What do you expect the bowel sounds to be on the stethoscope?

choices.label: Absent, because the bowel has stopped moving

say.text: Tempting: a blocked bowel feels dead, so silence seems to follow from a block.
But in mechanical obstruction peristalsis works against the block, so the sounds are hyperactive (K12, K61).
Silence points to adynamic obstruction or late peritonitis (K13, K61). What is right here: hyperactive, high-pitched, tinkling sounds (K61).

sure_note.text: You were sure silence means a blocked gut. Reverse it: a working gut against a block tinkles (K61).

say.text: Tempting: a distended, sluggish belly sounds like a gut that is failing, so the low pitch looks right.
But the bowel is not failing in a mechanical block. Peristalsis is working against the block, so sounds are hyperactive (K12, K61).
What is right: hyperactive, high-pitched, tinkling sounds (K61).

sure_note.text: You were sure the sounds would be low. Hold on to this: working bowel against a block is loud, not quiet (K61).

say.text: Right. Peristalsis works against a fixed block, so the sounds are hyperactive and tinkling (K12, K61).
A different patient. After laparotomy, on opioids, with distension and vomiting. The belly is silent on auscultation.
Most likely diagnosis?
Tempting: a distended, vomiting belly after surgery looks like a mechanical block.
But silence with distension and vomiting is the adynamic picture: peristalsis has failed (K13, K61).
What is right: paralytic ileus, with no peristalsis working against a block (K13).

sure_note.text: You were sure that silence means a block. Here silence means failed peristalsis (K13, K61).

say.text: Tempting: a twisted loop is a real mechanical block, so a mechanical label feels safe.
But the silent belly here means peristalsis has failed, not that it is working against a block (K61, K13).
What is right: paralytic ileus, the adynamic picture (K13).

sure_note.text: You were sure of a mechanical cause. A silent belly after surgery points to failed peristalsis (K61).

say.text: Right. A silent belly with distension and vomiting after surgery means failed peristalsis, so this is paralytic ileus (K13, K61).
A classmate says: 'Colic always means a simple block, so the pain never changes the plan.'
Known adhesive small bowel obstruction for two days. The colic has become constant and severe. Pulse 116, with tenderness over one loop. What does this suggest?

choices.label: Resolving obstruction, the colic is settling
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the word that changed in the pain, and at the pulse. What does that combination point to?
That is the classic colic picture, and it tempts because colic is the first symptom you learn (K49).
Hint: the word that changed matters more than the word colic. What does constant pain point to?
Pain that settles would fit a resolving block, which is why this option tempts. But check whether this pain is settling or changing.
Hint: count the systemic signs as well as the local ones.
Same patient, second look at the same findings. What does this suggest?

choices.label: Resolving obstruction, the colic is settling

say.text: Tempting: colic is the classic presentation, so a known adhesive block feels like a simple one (K49).
But pain that becomes constant and severe suggests strangulation (K50), and tachycardia with localised tenderness adds to it (K62).
What is right: strangulation needing urgent surgery, because the blood supply of the loop is compromised (K15).

sure_note.text: You were sure a known block stays simple. Keep this rule: constant, severe pain changes the plan (K50).

say.text: Tempting: a colic that eases looks like a block on its way out, so watching seems the next step.
But this pain is constant and severe, not settling. Constant severe pain suggests strangulation (K50), and fever, tachycardia and localised tenderness support it (K62).
What is right: strangulation needing urgent surgery, because the blood supply is compromised (K15).

sure_note.text: You were sure the pain was settling. Check the word: constant, not colicky (K50).

say.text: Right. Constant severe pain with tachycardia and localised tenderness suggests strangulation, and the blood supply is at risk (K50, K62, K15).
Final check on the signs. Which finding does NOT suggest strangulation?

choices.label: Constant severe pain with a normal pulse
Colicky central pain with normal tenderness
Pain that has settled into a steady ache

say.text: Tempting: constant pain sounds like colic that has simply lasted longer.
But constant, severe pain is itself a sign of strangulation (K50), and it sits with the other signs (K8).
What is right: colicky central pain with normal tenderness fits a simple block, and constant severe pain does not (K49, K50).
Tempting: a settled, steady ache looks like colic that is resolving, so it seems less urgent.
But constant pain is the change that points to strangulation (K50), and the dangerous signs come with it (K8).
What is right: colicky central pain with normal tenderness fits a simple block (K49).
Right. Colicky central pain with normal tenderness is the simple picture (K49). Strangulation comes with constant pain, fever, tachycardia, localised tenderness and a raised lactate (K8, K62, K67).
